narrative:
The model determined that you have an 82.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest reasons for the negative outcome. Being in the bottom decile for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3 pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. These rankings are far below the average of accepted students, who typically place around the middle of their class. Your LSAT score of 28 was the third most influential factor; it also pulled the prediction toward failure, as it sits well below the average of 37 among those who were accepted.

None of the other details, such as your middle family income, undergraduate GPA of 2.2, gender, race, or plan to attend full-time, played a meaningful role in the outcome. The system focused only on academic performance signals.

To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your academic standing and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Consider academic support programs, additional coursework, or test-prep resources before reapplying. Stronger performance in these areas would likely change the model’s prediction and open future opportunities. (218 words)
